newsitem.title: USA: Simpson due back on witness stand in civil trial.
newsitem.headline: Simpson due back on witness stand in civil trial.

text.p: O.J. Simpson returns to the witness stand on Monday to face more gentle questioning by his attorney, but the former American football star can also expect another round of harsh interrogation by opposing lawyers.

Testifying on Friday in a Santa Monica courtroom, Simpson denied ever hitting his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and spoke at length about their 17-year relationship. He ended the day by telling jurors that he loved her "very much."

But he also painted Nicole Brown Simpson as a woman who spun out of control after their 1992 divorce, using drugs, drinking heavily and partying with a fast crowd. And he said she pursued him for a reconciliation in 1993, which he agreed to only reluctantly.
Legal experts said it was risky for Simpson to criticise his dead ex-wife from the witness stand because the strategy might alienate some jurors.

Simpson, who was acquitted in October 1995 in the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend, Ronald Goldman, was one of the last defence witnesses expected to testify in a civil wrongful-death lawsuit brought by the victims' families.
Daniel Petrocelli, the lead lawyer for the plaintiffs, had called Simpson to the witness stand in November for more than two days of tough, often accusatory questioning.
Petrocelli is expected to take a similar approach when he cross-examines Simpson on Monday, though he will likely be barred by Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki from covering much of the same ground.

And Petrocelli has said he might call Simpson again in the rebuttal phase of the trial next week to confront him with 30 photographs taken at a pro football game in 1993 showing him wearing Italian designer Bruno Magli shoes.
Experts have testified that Bruno Magli soles were the ones that left a trail of bloody shoeprints leading from the murder scene outside Nicole Brown Simpson's apartment on June 12, 1994.
A defence photographic analyst testified that another photograph taken at the same game by a different photographer was a fake.
Under questioning on Friday by his attorney, Robert Baker, Simpson used an often matter-of-fact tone to describe in detail his long relationship with Nicole Brown Simpson.
But he didn't address much of the evidence that lawyers for the victims families contend link him to the murders.

For example, Baker did not ask Simpson to explain why his blood was found near the bodies outside Nicole Brown Simpson's condominium. Simpson also did not offer an explanation for why both victims' blood was found in his white Ford Bronco.
Defence attorneys, following the lead of Simpson's criminal trial lawyers, maintain that Simpson was framed by members of the Los Angeles Police Department.

Larry Schiller, who co-authored a book, "I Want to Tell You," with Simpson while he was in jail, then wrote a behind- the-scenes book about the defence team in the criminal case, was in court for Simpson's testimony on Friday and said the defendant was effective.
"He didn't come off as a liar," Schiller said. "He was believable."

When Simpson leaves the stand on Monday afternoon or Tuesday morning, the defence will have only a handful of witnesses left to call -- including Simpson's adult daughter, Arnelle -- before resting their case.

The plaintiffs' lawyers are then expected to present a brief rebuttal case before closing arguments begin, possibly as early as Friday. The case is expected to go to the jury before the end of the month.
